Cyber Security News
2026-06-11 3 use cases 0 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A China-linked network of compromised routers and smart devices has grown into one of the most capable reconnaissance tools tied to a nation-state threat group. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2b640582bbbffe58c4efb8ab5a0412e95130e70a587fd1e194fbcd4b33d432cf", "03c4667f016f1e8441177639d87f77a59f32d2c7e0041616376967338667bd3b", "1e0da906811b570c4134ade310c3a94631d4b308d27b616497266b49aae2ad0a", "d62055910cd579ff1fb57bd1926c5b2e80e1677f0316737b2f733f86b01615dc", "40ad28b87b5ed395fe8ff303555cc28974682ed6cc5a71ede76c4b17648cb8ed", "28a23ab78739de674f94d9acadfe0709862c2b2d947e9051b200a24d3f9f45c4", "d1414803a83b1ba260e3e1be742379eccbb806f987ec1e7c0bc5399e4971a58f", "96ecc107aa645e36b5f939ebfcf9e61fc9ebc27616680fbd0fdeb41c7950d79a") or SHA1 in~ ("2b640582bbbffe58c4efb8ab5a0412e95130e70a587fd1e194fbcd4b33d432cf", "03c4667f016f1e8441177639d87f77a59f32d2c7e0041616376967338667bd3b", "1e0da906811b570c4134ade310c3a94631d4b308d27b616497266b49aae2ad0a", "d62055910cd579ff1fb57bd1926c5b2e80e1677f0316737b2f733f86b01615dc", "40ad28b87b5ed395fe8ff303555cc28974682ed6cc5a71ede76c4b17648cb8ed", "28a23ab78739de674f94d9acadfe0709862c2b2d947e9051b200a24d3f9f45c4", "d1414803a83b1ba260e3e1be742379eccbb806f987ec1e7c0bc5399e4971a58f", "96ecc107aa645e36b5f939ebfcf9e61fc9ebc27616680fbd0fdeb41c7950d79a") or MD5 in~ ("2b640582bbbffe58c4efb8ab5a0412e95130e70a587fd1e194fbcd4b33d432cf", "03c4667f016f1e8441177639d87f77a59f32d2c7e0041616376967338667bd3b", "1e0da906811b570c4134ade310c3a94631d4b308d27b616497266b49aae2ad0a", "d62055910cd579ff1fb57bd1926c5b2e80e1677f0316737b2f733f86b01615dc", "40ad28b87b5ed395fe8ff303555cc28974682ed6cc5a71ede76c4b17648cb8ed", "28a23ab78739de674f94d9acadfe0709862c2b2d947e9051b200a24d3f9f45c4", "d1414803a83b1ba260e3e1be742379eccbb806f987ec1e7c0bc5399e4971a58f", "96ecc107aa645e36b5f939ebfcf9e61fc9ebc27616680fbd0fdeb41c7950d79a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2b640582bbbffe58c4efb8ab5a0412e95130e70a587fd1e194fbcd4b33d432cf", "03c4667f016f1e8441177639d87f77a59f32d2c7e0041616376967338667bd3b", "1e0da906811b570c4134ade310c3a94631d4b308d27b616497266b49aae2ad0a", "d62055910cd579ff1fb57bd1926c5b2e80e1677f0316737b2f733f86b01615dc", "40ad28b87b5ed395fe8ff303555cc28974682ed6cc5a71ede76c4b17648cb8ed", "28a23ab78739de674f94d9acadfe0709862c2b2d947e9051b200a24d3f9f45c4", "d1414803a83b1ba260e3e1be742379eccbb806f987ec1e7c0bc5399e4971a58f", "96ecc107aa645e36b5f939ebfcf9e61fc9ebc27616680fbd0fdeb41c7950d79a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Exchange Server 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks Using Weaponized Email

Cyber Security News
2026-06-11 1 use case 0 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation of a new zero‑day spoofing flaw in on‑premises Exchange Server, tracked as CVE‑2026‑42897. The flaw allows attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in Outlook Web Access (OWA) simply by sending a weaponized email that a victim opens in a browser. On May 14, 2026, Microsoft disclosed CVE‑2026‑42897 as a spoofing vulnerability [&#8230;] The post Microsoft Exchange Server 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks Using Weaponized Email appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] HTTP POST to Oracle PeopleSoft deserialization endpoints (gadget chain initial access) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PeopleSoft Tuxedo / Java app-server spawning shells (post-exploit RCE)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection or DNS to ShinyHunters PeopleSoft campaign infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Large outbound HTTPS upload from PeopleSoft application or database server · [LLM] Bulk SELECT or export from PeopleSoft student / finance tables
HTTP POST to Oracle PeopleSoft deserialization endpoints (gadget chain initial access) AIExploitation Medium
Detects POST requests targeting Oracle PeopleSoft (PSFT) Tuxedo/PIA endpoints that are commonly abused by ShinyHunters' 'gadget chain' of zero-day + known deserialization bugs. Focuses on PeopleSoft-specific URI stems and oversized request bodies indicative of serialized Java payloads. Rationale: Targets the PeopleSoft 'gadget chain' explicitly named in the article. PSFT-specific URI stems (/psp/, /psc/, /PSIGW/, IntegrationGateway) + oversized POST bodies are the signature of Java/Tuxedo deserialization exploits. Cross-checked Oracle CPU advisories and prior CVE-2023-22054 / CVE-2023-22102 PeopleSoft deserialization research. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1024/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleSoft integration broker traffic from partner systems (HR, payroll, SIS connectors)
  • PeopleTools upgrade installers POSTing large payloads to /psc/
  • Internal load testing against PIA endpoints
  • Mobile PeopleSoft Fluid UI POSTs containing large form payloads
  • Legitimate large file uploads via PeopleSoft attachment service
Suppression filter
and cIP !in ("<partner_integration_ip_1>","<partner_integration_ip_2>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull full request body via WAF/reverse proxy for the matched POST; look for Java serialization magic bytes (AC ED 00 05), gadget-class names (CommonsBeanutils, Tuxedo PSFT_*), or readObject markers. Confirm caller IP is not in the partner integration allowlist. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the edge WAF; if exploitation indicators present, isolate the PSFT app-server VM and snapshot for forensics; rotate any service-account credentials with PSFT DB access. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot from the PSFT host on DeviceProcessEvents for child processes of PSAPPSRV/PSPRCSRV/java.exe; query DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to 142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24, or azurenetfiles.net; check DB audit logs for bulk SELECT on PS_STUDENT_/PS_FINANCE_ tables.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("PSAPPSRV.exe","PSPRCSRV.exe","tuxedo.exe","java.exe","javaw.exe","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80,443,8000,8080,8443,7777)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/psp/","/psc/","/PSIGW/","/peoplesoft/","/cs/ps/","PeopleSoftServiceListeningConnector","IntegrationGateway")
| where csBytes > 50000 or csUriStem has_any ("PeopleSoftServiceListeningConnector","IntegrationGateway")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, csBytes, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 5a8e1d2c-4f7b-4c9a-9e2f-1b3d4a6c7e8d
description: Detects POST requests to known PeopleSoft PIA/Tuxedo/IntegrationGateway endpoints associated with the ShinyHunters PeopleSoft gadget-chain campaign that breached University of Nottingham and 100+ orgs.

      - 'IntegrationGateway'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:(windows.security OR linux.syslog) (@http.method:POST OR @CommandLine:POST) (@http.url:(*\/psp\/* OR *\/psc\/* OR *\/PSIGW\/* OR *\/peoplesoft\/* OR *PeopleSoftServiceListeningConnector* OR *IntegrationGateway*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ConnectionDirection=1
| ContextImageFileName=/(PSAPPSRV|PSPRCSRV|tuxedo|java|javaw|w3wp|httpd|nginx)\.exe$/i
| RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=8000 OR RemotePort=8080 OR RemotePort=8443 OR RemotePort=7777

WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.src) as src values(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST (Web.url="*/psp/*" OR Web.url="*/psc/*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW/*" OR Web.url="*/peoplesoft/*" OR Web.url="*/cs/ps/*") (Web.bytes_in>50000 OR Web.url="*PeopleSoftServiceListeningConnector*" OR Web.url="*IntegrationGateway*") by Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status<500
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.src) as src values(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST (Web.url="*/psp/*" OR Web.url="*/psc/*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW/*" OR Web.url="*/peoplesoft/*" OR Web.url="*/cs/ps/*") (Web.bytes_in>50000 OR Web.url="*PeopleSoftServiceListeningConnector*" OR Web.url="*IntegrationGateway*") by Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status<500
PeopleSoft Tuxedo / Java app-server spawning shells (post-exploit RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the textbook deserialization RCE outcome: PeopleSoft PSAPPSRV/PSPRCSRV/Tuxedo/java processes spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, /bin/sh, or staging tools. This is the execution stage of the ShinyHunters PeopleSoft gadget-chain campaign. Rationale: Article states 'gadget chain of zero-days and old vulnerabilities' resulting in RCE on PeopleSoft. PeopleSoft application server processes (PSAPPSRV, PSPRCSRV, Tuxedo BBL) spawning a shell or LOLBin is a near-zero-FP indicator of successful deserialization exploitation. This is the canonical execution-phase pivot for PeopleSoft compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1024/ • https://docs.oracle.com/cd/F69094_01/pt860pbr5/eng/pt/tsvr/concept_PeopleSoftServerProcesses.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PeopleSoft Application Engine programs legitimately calling cmd.exe wrappers for OS file operations
  • SQR/COBOL batch jobs invoking shells for archive cleanup
  • PeopleSoft DBA scripts run via PSADMIN for legitimate maintenance
  • Oracle PeopleTools patch installers spawning command shells
  • Custom shell-out logic in legacy Application Engine PeopleCode
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSADMIN","AE_DAEMON","PTUPGRADE") and AccountName endswith "_psadmin")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full command line of the child process; check for download/exec patterns (Invoke-WebRequest, IEX, certutil -urlcache, base64). Correlate with W3CIISLog for an incoming POST to /psp/, /psc/, /PSIGW/, or IntegrationGateway in the preceding 60s. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the PeopleSoft host with EDR network containment; suspend PSAPPSRV service to stop further child-process spawning; snapshot for forensics. Rotate the PSFT service-account password and DB credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all PSFT app-server fleet for the same parent->child pattern in the last 30 days; query DeviceFileEvents for archives (.zip/.7z/.tar) written by PSAPPSRV/java in the past week; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to the campaign IPs/domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("PSAPPSRV.exe","PSPRCSRV.exe","PSADMIN.exe","tuxedo.exe","tmboot.exe","BBL.exe","java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","sh","bash","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("PSAPPSRV.exe","PSPRCSRV.exe","PSADMIN.exe","tuxedo.exe","tmboot.exe","BBL.exe","java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection or DNS to ShinyHunters PeopleSoft campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for any host (especially application/database server VLANs) contacting the ShinyHunters campaign IP block 142.11.200.186-190, the supporting addresses 108.174.202.99 / 176.120.22.24, or DNS lookups for azurenetfiles.net used by the actor for staging/exfiltration of stolen PeopleSoft data. Rationale: Article ships explicit IOC IPs (142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24) and the lookalike domain azurenetfiles.net used by ShinyHunters in the PeopleSoft campaign. Any contact from an internal host — particularly server VLANs hosting PeopleSoft — is high-confidence indicator of compromise. Cross-checked phase 5/6 IOC block from kill-chain reconstruction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nottingham-university-data-breach-affects-over-450-000-students/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning hosts deliberately probing campaign IPs for telemetry
  • Researcher VMs running sandbox detonations against the IOCs
  • Honeypot infrastructure attracting attacker callbacks
  • Lookalike-domain typosquat reports - 'azurenetfiles.net' may resemble legit azurewebsites.net so misconfigured DNS forwarders could query
  • Legitimate Azure file storage requests mistyped to azurenetfiles.net
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "honeypot-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the contacting host, its VLAN/role (is it a PeopleSoft app or DB server?), and the initiating process. Pull a 24h timeline of egress bytes from the host to detect bulk exfil. Step 2 (contain): EDR network-isolate the host; block the IP block 142.11.200.0/24 + 108.174.202.99 + 176.120.22.24 at perimeter firewall; sinkhole azurenetfiles.net at internal DNS. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep CommonSecurityLog/DeviceNetworkEvents fleet-wide for the same IOCs over 90d; pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for PSAPPSRV/java spawning archive utilities (7z, zip, tar) preceding the egress; check DB audit logs for bulk PII queries on the same host.
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["azurenetfiles.net"]);
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (CampaignIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| union (DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where AdditionalFields has "azurenetfiles.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["azurenetfiles.net"]);
(CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP in (CampaignIPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (CampaignDomains) or RequestURL has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceAction, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes)
| union (DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (CampaignDomains)

| union (ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (CampaignIPs) or DstHostname has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Large outbound HTTPS upload from PeopleSoft application or database server AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for sustained multi-gigabyte outbound transfers from servers hosting Oracle PeopleSoft (PSFT) to non-corporate destinations — matches the 40GB+ exfiltration profile claimed by ShinyHunters against Nottingham and 100+ orgs. Rationale: Article quantifies the exfil: '40GB of documents containing student finance data, billing and payment information, credit card and payment details, and campus portal exports'. Combining a PeopleSoft/Oracle/archive-utility source process with sustained multi-GB outbound HTTPS to public destinations matches the campaign's exfil profile across all 100+ victims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nottingham-university-data-breach-affects-over-450-000-students/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleSoft data warehouse exports to a cloud SFTP partner
  • Database backup uploads to S3/Azure Blob from Oracle hosts
  • Veeam/CommVault cloud-tier backup egress
  • Legitimate ETL jobs pushing transformed PeopleSoft data to a BI cloud (Snowflake, BigQuery)
  • WSUS/SCCM cache sync from server VLAN
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName !endswith ".amazonaws.com" and DestinationHostName !endswith ".blob.core.windows.net" and DestinationHostName !endswith ".veeam.com" and DestinationHostName !endswith ".commvault.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source host's role (PSFT app, PSFT DB, ETL gateway?) and the destination autonomous system / ASN owner. Compare the egress volume against the host's 30-day P95 baseline. Step 2 (contain): If the destination is not on the corporate allow-list (cloud backup endpoints, known SFTP partners), EDR-isolate the host; block destination at perimeter; preserve memory + disk for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for recent archive-creation activity (7z/rar/tar) on the same host; query DB audit logs for bulk SELECT on PS_STUDENT_/PS_FINANCE_ tables in the preceding 24h; check for child processes of PSAPPSRV/java spawning curl/powershell with Invoke-WebRequest.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("PSAPPSRV.exe","PSPRCSRV.exe","tuxedo.exe","java.exe","javaw.exe","oracle.exe","tnslsnr.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","WinRAR.exe","rar.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize ConnectionCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Destinations = make_set(RemoteIP, 50), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where ConnectionCount > 100
| order by ConnectionCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in ("Palo Alto Networks","Fortinet","Cisco","Check Point","Zscaler")
| where CommunicationDirection in ("outbound","1","Outbound") or isnotempty(DestinationIP)
| where SourceHostName has_any ("psft","peoplesoft","-ps-","-orcl","-tux") or SourceIP startswith "10." 
| summarize TotalBytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)), Connections = count() by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where TotalBytesOut > 1073741824
| extend GB_Out = round(todouble(TotalBytesOut)/1073741824, 2)
| order by TotalBytesOut desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:3 @Image:(*\PSAPPSRV.exe OR *\psappsrv.exe OR *\PSPRCSRV.exe OR *\java.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\tuxedo.exe OR *\7z.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe) @DestinationPort:(443 OR 80 OR 8443) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/(PSAPPSRV|PSPRCSRV|tuxedo|java|javaw|oracle|tnslsnr|7z|7za|WinRAR|rar|curl|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=8443
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
| count > 100
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, bytes, action
| filter action = "ACCEPT" and dstPort in [443, 80, 8443]
| filter not (dstAddr like /^10\./ or dstAddr like /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\./ or dstAddr like /^192\.168\./)
| stats sum(bytes) as total_bytes_out by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, bin(1h) as hour
| filter total_bytes_out > 1073741824
| sort total_bytes_out desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as total_bytes_out count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=ssl OR All_Traffic.dest_port IN (443,80,8443) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search src="*psft*" OR src="*peoplesoft*" OR src="*-ps-*" OR src="*-orcl*" OR src="*-tux*" | where total_bytes_out > 1073741824 | eval gb_out=round(total_bytes_out/1073741824,2) | table src dest_ip dest gb_out count
Bulk SELECT or export from PeopleSoft student / finance tables AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for bulk read access against PeopleSoft student-record and finance tables (PS_STUDENT_*, PS_STDNT_*, PS_FIN_*, PS_CC_*) — the exact data classes ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen from Nottingham (names, addresses, passport numbers, fee/payment data, credit-card details). Rationale: Article explicitly enumerates the stolen data classes: 'student finance data, billing and payment information, credit card and payment details, and campus portal exports' plus 'names, addresses, phone numbers, ethnicities, disabilities, passport numbers'. PeopleSoft canonical table prefixes for this data are PS_STUDENT_*, PS_STDNT_*, PS_FIN_*, PS_CC_* (credit card), PS_PAYMENT_*, PS_BILLING_*. Bulk SELECT against these by an unusual user/host is high signal. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E83876_01/psft/index.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nottingham-university-data-breach-affects-over-450-000-students/
ATT&CKT1213 T1005 T1560
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate financial-aid reporting jobs by University finance staff
  • Term-end batch billing runs touching PS_BILLING / PS_FIN tables
  • Regulatory reporting exports (HESA, IRS-1098T, ICEF) hitting student tables
  • DBA-led PS_STUDENT_* table cardinality analysis during a PeopleTools upgrade
  • BI / data-warehouse ETL pulling nightly snapshots of student records
Suppression filter
| where DB_USER !in ("REPORTING_SVC","ETL_SVC","HESA_REPORT") and CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME !in ("informatica","ssis","talend")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the executing DB user, OS user, and client program; compare against the list of approved ETL/finance batch jobs and reporting service accounts. Confirm the host generating the SELECTs is a sanctioned BI/ETL host, not a PSFT app server unexpectedly running ad-hoc queries. Step 2 (contain): If the source is the PSFT app server itself (PSAPPSRV/java initiating the SELECTs out-of-band), revoke the session, kill the DB session, isolate the host, rotate the PSFT service-account password and Oracle DB credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for archive/CSV creation by the same process; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound from the host to the campaign IPs (142.11.200.0/24, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24) or azurenetfiles.net; sweep PSFT fleet for the same query pattern in the prior 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("PSAPPSRV.exe","PSPRCSRV.exe","java.exe","javaw.exe","oracle.exe","sqlplus.exe","expdp.exe","exp.exe","sqlcmd.exe")
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".csv" or FileName endswith ".dmp" or FileName endswith ".sql" or FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".7z" or FileName endswith ".rar" or FileName endswith ".tar" or FileName endswith ".gz" or FileName endswith ".xlsx"
| where FileSize > 50000000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize
| order by FileSize desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Facility in ("local0","local1","daemon") or ProcessName has "oracle"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("PS_STUDENT","PS_STDNT","PS_FIN_","PS_CC_","PS_PAYMENT","PS_BILLING")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("SELECT","EXPORT","EXPDP")
| extend TablesTouched = extract_all(@"PS_[A-Z_]+", SyslogMessage)
| summarize EventCount = count(), DistinctTables = dcount_array(TablesTouched), Tables = make_set(TablesTouched, 50) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where EventCount > 50 or DistinctTables > 5
| order by EventCount desc
source:(linux.syslog OR linux.auditd OR windows.sysmon) (PS_STUDENT* OR PS_STDNT* OR PS_FIN_* OR PS_CC_* OR PS_PAYMENT* OR PS_BILLING*) (SELECT OR EXPORT OR expdp OR exp)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(PSAPPSRV|PSPRCSRV|java|javaw|oracle|sqlplus|expdp|exp|sqlcmd)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(csv|dmp|sql|zip|7z|rar|tar|gz|xlsx)$/i
| WrittenBytes>50000000
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
CLOUD
index=oracle_audit OR sourcetype="oracle:audit" OR sourcetype="db:audit" (action_name=SELECT OR statement=SELECT*) (OBJECT_NAME="PS_STUDENT*" OR OBJECT_NAME="PS_STDNT*" OR OBJECT_NAME="PS_FIN_*" OR OBJECT_NAME="PS_CC_*" OR OBJECT_NAME="PS_PAYMENT*" OR OBJECT_NAME="PS_BILLING*" OR SQL_TEXT="*PS_STUDENT*" OR SQL_TEXT="*PS_STDNT*" OR SQL_TEXT="*PS_FIN_*" OR SQL_TEXT="*PS_CC_*") | stats count dc(OBJECT_NAME) as tables_touched values(OBJECT_NAME) as tables sum(rows_processed) as total_rows by DB_USER OS_USER USERHOST CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME | where tables_touched > 5 OR total_rows > 100000 | sort - total_rows
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced what it said are "breaking changes" coming to npm version 12, one of which turns off install scripts by default to combat software supply chain threats. The changes aim to combat attack techniques that abuse the "npm install" command to trigger the execution of malicious code using npm lifecycle hooks. "Npm install" is used to download and install all the necessary

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unpatched Ivanti Sentry appliances exposed to CVE-2026-10520 AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts still running pre-R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1 Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) with CVE-2026-10520 (and the related CVE-2026-10523) still unpatched. Shadowserver reports widespread compromise of any unpatched Sentry that is internet-reachable, so this is the patch-status hunt that should run before the C2 hunt below. Rationale: Anchored on the exact CVE IDs from the article (CVE-2026-10520 + the sibling CVE-2026-10523 the BleepingComputer piece reuses) and the fixed-version strings Ivanti published (R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1). Cross-checked with Shadowserver's stat that ~all internet-exposed Sentry instances are likely backdoored, so IsInternetFacing is the priority pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.shadowserver.org/ • https://forums.ivanti.com/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-10520
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VM scanner snapshot lagging behind a freshly-patched Sentry node (status still reads vulnerable for ~24h)
  • Decommissioned Sentry VM still in CMDB but powered off and unreachable
  • Test/lab Sentry instance intentionally kept on R10.4.x for regression testing
  • Air-gapped Sentry behind an internal-only VIP showing as 'IsInternetFacing=false' but flagged anyway
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "R10.5.2" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "R10.6.2" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "R10.7.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SoftwareVersion column shows a build below R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1 — Ivanti backported the fix into all three trains. Cross-check IsInternetFacing/PublicIP against external attack-surface scans. 2) Contain: ACL the Sentry admin VIP to corporate IPs only and force-upgrade. If the appliance was internet-reachable for >24h after CVE disclosure, treat as compromised per Shadowserver guidance — pull config, rotate any AD bind/service creds, force-reissue device certificates. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC #2 (anomalous outbound) on each vulnerable hostId, and dump /var/log on the Sentry filesystem for backdoor implants or new SUID binaries written since the disclosure date.

Anomalous outbound connection from Ivanti Sentry appliance (CVE-2026-10520 backdoor) AICommand & Control High
Sentry appliances are management gateways; their outbound traffic profile is narrow (Ivanti cloud, NTP, DNS, syslog forwarder, MDM back-end). Shadowserver reports the CVE-2026-10520 PoC is being used to drop backdoors on most internet-exposed Sentry boxes — so any Sentry initiating a connection to a non-allowlisted public IP, especially on a non-standard port, is a strong post-exploitation indicator. Rationale: Pivot is the article's own framing: Shadowserver observed Sentry boxes being backdoored at scale via the public PoC for CVE-2026-10520, but the article gives no IOC hashes or specific C2 domains — so the highest-fidelity signal is a behavioural one (Sentry initiating outbound to non-allowlisted public IP/port). Allowed-ports set covers the standard Sentry egress (Ivanti telemetry, NTP, syslog, MDM HTTPS, admin HTTPS). Cross-checked against: • https://www.shadowserver.org/ • https://forums.ivanti.com/community/security-advisories
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly-onboarded Sentry pulling firmware/AV updates from a CDN edge IP on port 8080
  • Sentry forwarding telemetry to a SaaS log aggregator (Datadog/Sumo) on a non-standard port
  • Operator opening an outbound support tunnel to Ivanti TSE on a temporary port
  • Sentry reaching out to an externally-hosted CA/OCSP responder on port 80/443 (filtered, but URL-list edge cases)
  • MDM back-end reachable only via SaaS over port 8081 in some Sentry topologies
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("<ivanti-cloud-cidrs>","<your-mdm-saas-ip>") or RemoteUrl has_any ("ivanti.com","mobileiron.com","<sanctioned-log-saas-domain>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DeviceName is actually a Sentry appliance (not a host with 'sentry' in its hostname). Resolve the destination IP — is it Ivanti-owned, a known SaaS partner, or unattributed/VPS? Pull the same Sentry's syslog around the connect time for /mics or /authservice HTTP POSTs preceding the egress. 2) Contain: drop the Sentry's outbound at the perimeter (deny rule on DestinationIP), snapshot the appliance, and isolate from the corporate VLAN. 3) Hunt: across all Sentry boxes, summarize unique RemoteIP+RemotePort destinations over 30d — anything matching the new IP is the same backdoor. Also check for new files in /tmp, new cron entries, and new SSH authorized_keys on the appliance; rotate any AD bind, certificate, and API tokens the Sentry holds.
let SentryDevices = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where Vendor has "Ivanti" or DeviceName has "sentry" or DeviceName has "mobileiron" or OSDistribution has "sentry"
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
let AllowedPorts = dynamic([53, 80, 123, 443, 514, 8443]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (SentryDevices)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort !in (AllowedPorts)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), SampleProcess=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by FirstSeen desc
let SentryHosts = Heartbeat
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where Computer has "sentry" or Computer has "mobileiron"
    | distinct Computer;
let AllowedPorts = dynamic([53, 80, 123, 443, 514, 8443]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SourceHostName in (SentryHosts) or SourceUserName in (SentryHosts)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","accept","permit")
| where DestinationPort !in (AllowedPorts)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count() by SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc
(source:linux.syslog OR source:windows.sysmon) (@host:(*sentry* OR *SENTRY* OR *Sentry* OR *mobileiron* OR *MobileIron*)) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 192.168.0.0/16) -@network.destination.port:(53 OR 80 OR 123 OR 443 OR 514 OR 8443)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ComputerName=/sentry|mobileiron/i
| RemotePort!=53 RemotePort!=80 RemotePort!=123 RemotePort!=443 RemotePort!=514 RemotePort!=8443
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| _count > 0

Langflow CVE-2026-5027 path-traversal POST to /api/v2/files AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP POST requests to Langflow's vulnerable /api/v2/files endpoint carrying path-traversal markers in the URL/query or originating from non-browser scanner user-agents. Targets the active exploitation pattern reported by VulnCheck honeypots. Rationale: Targets the exact vulnerable endpoint (/api/v2/files) and HTTP verb (POST) named in Tenable's advisory and the article. Adds URL-encoded traversal variants (%2e%2e%2f / %252e%252e%252f) plus scanner user-agents commonly observed in VulnCheck honeypot exploitation. Defender query is intentionally narrow (port + Langflow process) since EDR cannot inspect HTTP bodies.
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7) probing Langflow as part of authorised scans
  • CI/CD pipelines using curl or python-requests to upload flow definitions to a corporate Langflow instance
  • Legitimate ML engineers using the Langflow Python SDK (UA includes 'python-requests') against authorised internal hosts
  • Security research traffic from the org's own bug-bounty or red-team scope
  • Langflow's own integration tests run from the host's own subnet
Suppression filter
// Sentinel — suppress known scanners and CI/CD pipelines once allow-listed:
// | where SrcIP !in ("<corp_scanner_subnet>") and UA !contains "<corp_ci_agent_signature>"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full POST body from WAF/proxy (if body logging is enabled) and confirm the multipart 'filename' field contains '../'. Check the response status — 200/201 means the write likely succeeded. Verify the Langflow instance version: anything pre-1.9.0 (or langflow-base pre-0.8.3) is vulnerable. Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge. Take the Langflow instance offline if it's externally exposed and unpatched; restrict the listener to localhost or a VPN. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (Langflow file writes) on the same host within ±5 min of the POST; check /etc/cron*, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, /var/www/, /etc/ld.so.preload for new entries; review outbound connections from the python/uvicorn process for reverse-shell beacons; cross-check the source IP against MuddyWater infra given the prior CVE-2025-3248 linkage.
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no HTTP request-body visibility; this UC primarily targets W3C/WAF logs (see sentinel_kql). The closest Defender pivot is inbound network connections to the Langflow listener on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (7860, 3000, 8000, 8080)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "langflow_base", "langflow.main")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), Sources=make_set(RemoteIP, 50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| where ConnCount > 5
| order by ConnCount desc
// Covers IIS/AppService and WAF/reverse-proxy via CommonSecurityLog
let traversal_re = @"(?i)(\.\./|%2e%2e%2f|%252e%252e%252f|\.\.%5c|\.\.\\\\)";
let scanner_ua_re = @"(?i)(curl|python-requests|go-http-client|nuclei|nmap|wget|httpx|fuzz|gobuster)";
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csMethod =~ "POST"
  | where csUriStem has "/api/v2/files"
  | extend SrcIP=cIP, URL=strcat(csUriStem,"?",csUriQuery), UA=csUserAgent, Status=tostring(scStatus), Source="IIS")
| union
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
  | where RequestURL has "/api/v2/files" or Message has "/api/v2/files"
  | extend SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, UA=RequestClientApplication, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), Source=strcat(DeviceVendor,"/",DeviceProduct))
| union
(AppServiceHTTPLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where CsMethod =~ "POST"
  | where CsUriStem has "/api/v2/files"
  | extend SrcIP=CIp, URL=strcat(CsUriStem,"?",CsUriQuery), UA=UserAgent, Status=tostring(ScStatus), Source="AppService")
| extend TraversalMarker = iff(URL matches regex traversal_re, true, false)
| extend ScannerUA = iff(UA matches regex scanner_ua_re, true, false)
| where TraversalMarker == true or ScannerUA == true or Status startswith "2"
| summarize Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), URLs=make_set(URL, 10), UAs=make_set(UA, 10), Statuses=make_set(Status, 10), Markers=make_set(pack("traversal",TraversalMarker,"scanner_ua",ScannerUA),5) by SrcIP, Source
| order by Hits desc

    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - '../'
      - '..%2f'
      - '%2e%2e%2f'
      - '%252e%252e'
      - '..%5c'
  selection_scanner_ua:
    c-useragent|contains:
      - 'curl/'
      - 'python-requests'
      - 'Go-http-client'
      - 'nuclei'
      - 'wget/'
      - 'httpx'
  condition: selection_endpoint and (selection_traversal or selection_scanner_ua)
falsepositives:
  - Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Nessus) probing the endpoint
  - Legitimate CI/CD pipelines uploading flow files via Langflow API
level: high
source:(nginx OR apache OR aws.alb OR azure.frontdoor OR cloudflare) @http.method:POST @http.url_details.path:*\/api\/v2\/files* (@http.url:(*..%2F* OR *..%2f* OR *%2e%2e%2f* OR *..\/* ) OR @http.useragent:(*curl* OR *python-requests* OR *Go-http-client* OR *nuclei* OR *wget* OR *httpx*))
// Falcon EDR has no HTTP body inspection — this approximates by surfacing the Langflow listener accepting public connections; pair with proxy/WAF telemetry for body-level traversal markers.
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1
| LocalPort=/^(7860|3000|8000|8080)$/
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)/i CommandLine=/langflow/i}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], key=[aid, TargetProcessId], include=[ImageFileName, CommandLine])

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, LocalPort], function=[count(as=hits), count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=unique_src_ips)])
| hits > 5
# log group: /aws/applicationloadbalancer (point at the ALB fronting Langflow; for CloudFront use /aws/cloudfront)

Langflow auto-login token issuance followed by /api/v2/files POST within seconds AIExploitation High
Detects the credential_access pattern unique to CVE-2026-5027 exploitation: an external IP hits Langflow's unauthenticated auto-login endpoint to mint a session token, then immediately POSTs to /api/v2/files. This single-IP burst pattern is the lowest-effort exploit signature and is the shape VulnCheck honeypots describe. Rationale: Captures the exploit kill chain the VulnCheck post describes — a single unauthenticated session-token mint immediately followed by the file upload. The 30-second window matches scripted exploit cadence; legitimate users take longer between login and first action. Article quote: 'a single unauthenticated request is sufficient to obtain a valid session token before proceeding with exploitation'.
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1539 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users behind a shared NAT egressing from one corporate IP — login then immediate API usage
  • Automated CI/CD pipelines calling auto_login then file upload as part of nightly flow-deployment jobs
  • Vulnerability scanners that intentionally script the login+endpoint sequence to test reachability
  • Selenium / Playwright smoke tests against staging Langflow that mimic this exact pattern
  • Langflow's own integration test suite hitting localhost
Suppression filter
// Suppress known internal CI ranges (Sentinel): | where SrcIP !in ("<corp_ci_egress_ip_1>","<corp_ci_egress_ip_2>")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and not on the corporate egress list. Pull the full request chain — was the login a 200 with a new session cookie? Was the file POST a 200/201 (write succeeded) or 400 (rejected)? Step 2 — Contain: Block the IP at the WAF, force-rotate any Langflow session signing keys, and patch the instance to 1.10.0 immediately (1.9.0 also fixes 5027 but 1.10.0 is the latest as of the article). Disable auto-login by setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false. Step 3 — Hunt: Look for the same SrcIP in the prior 30 days to spot reconnaissance; correlate with UC3 (file writes by python/uvicorn outside upload dir) on the host hosting Langflow within 60s of the upload event.
// Defender Advanced Hunting cannot see HTTP request paths; the correlation lives at the proxy/WAF layer. See sentinel_kql.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30s;
let WebReqs = union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback) | extend SrcIP=cIP, URL=csUriStem, Method=csMethod, Status=tostring(scStatus), Source="IIS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback) | extend SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), Source=DeviceProduct),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback) | extend SrcIP=CIp, URL=CsUriStem, Method=CsMethod, Status=tostring(ScStatus), Source="AppService")
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP, URL, Method, Status, Source;
let Logins = WebReqs | where URL has_any ("/api/v1/auto_login", "/api/v1/login") | project LoginTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIP, LoginURL=URL, LoginStatus=Status, Source;
let Uploads = WebReqs | where URL has "/api/v2/files" and Method =~ "POST" | project UploadTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIP, UploadURL=URL, UploadStatus=Status;
Logins
| join kind=inner Uploads on SrcIP
| where UploadTime between (LoginTime .. LoginTime + window)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', UploadTime, LoginTime)
| summarize Pairs=count(), FirstLogin=min(LoginTime), FirstUpload=min(UploadTime), MinDelay=min(DelaySec), URLs=make_set(UploadURL, 5) by SrcIP, Source
| where Pairs >= 1
| order by MinDelay asc
source:(nginx OR apache OR aws.alb OR azure.frontdoor OR cloudflare) (@http.url_details.path:*\/api\/v1\/auto_login* OR (@http.method:POST AND @http.url_details.path:*\/api\/v2\/files*))
# log group: /aws/applicationloadbalancer (point at the ALB fronting Langflow)
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_verb, request_url, elb_status_code
| filter request_url like /\/api\/v1\/auto_login/ or (request_verb = "POST" and request_url like /\/api\/v2\/files/)
| stats count(*) as hits, earliest(@timestamp) as first_hit, latest(@timestamp) as last_hit, count_distinct(request_url) as distinct_urls by client_ip, bin(1m)
| filter distinct_urls >= 2 and hits >= 2
| sort first_hit desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*api/v1/auto_login*" OR Web.url="*api/v1/login*" OR (Web.url="*api/v2/files*" AND Web.http_method=POST)) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.status _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval action=case(match(url,"(?i)auto_login|/login"),"login", match(url,"(?i)api/v2/files") AND http_method="POST","upload", true(),"other")
| where action!="other"
| sort 0 src _time
| streamstats window=2 values(action) as actions values(_time) as times values(url) as urls values(status) as statuses by src dest
| where mvcount(actions)=2 AND mvindex(actions,0)="login" AND mvindex(actions,1)="upload"
| eval delay_sec=mvindex(times,1)-mvindex(times,0)
| where delay_sec <= 30
| eval login_time=strftime(mvindex(times,0),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), upload_time=strftime(mvindex(times,1),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| table src dest login_time upload_time delay_sec urls statuses
| sort - delay_sec
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*api/v1/auto_login*" OR Web.url="*api/v1/login*" OR (Web.url="*api/v2/files*" AND Web.http_method=POST)) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.status _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval action=case(match(url,"(?i)auto_login|/login"),"login", match(url,"(?i)api/v2/files") AND http_method="POST","upload", true(),"other")
| where action!="other"
| sort 0 src _time
| streamstats window=2 values(action) as actions values(_time) as times values(url) as urls values(status) as statuses by src dest

| eval login_time=strftime(mvindex(times,0),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), upload_time=strftime(mvindex(times,1),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| table src dest login_time upload_time delay_sec urls statuses
| sort - delay_sec
Langflow python/uvicorn process writing files outside expected data directory AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation file-write side-effect of CVE-2026-5027: the Langflow service (python / uvicorn / gunicorn running 'langflow') drops files into directories outside its normal upload/data path — particularly into cron, SSH key, web-root, library-preload, or systemd unit paths. Matches the VulnCheck-reported behaviour of attackers dropping marker/test files via path traversal. Rationale: Pivots on the exact process Langflow runs as (python/uvicorn/gunicorn with 'langflow' in cmdline) and the file-write side-effect named in the kill chain: 'Watch for the Langflow process (python/uvicorn) writing files to paths outside its expected upload/data directories, especially into /etc, /root, cron paths, or web roots.' Explicitly filters out the legitimate Langflow data directory to keep precision high.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1565.001 T1098.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow first-run setup writing default config to /root/.langflow/ if running as root (filtered)
  • Custom Langflow components that legitimately export artefacts to /usr/local/share or /tmp
  • pip install run inside the Langflow venv writing console_scripts shims into /usr/local/bin
  • Container image build writing layers to /etc/profile.d (build-time, not runtime — distinguish via process ancestry)
  • Admin SSH'd into the host running ad-hoc python scripts named 'langflow_something.py' that legitimately touch system paths
Suppression filter
// Tighten by requiring the file write to be NEW (not modification of an existing file the process legitimately owns):
// Defender: | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
// Sentinel ImFileEvent: | where EventType == "FileCreated"
// And exclude package-install paths if Langflow pip-installs at runtime:
// | where not(InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("pip", "pip3", "poetry", "uv"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Read the written file's contents immediately (cat) and SHA-256 hash it; check if it's a webshell, a cron entry calling out, an SSH key for an unknown user, or an ld.so.preload library. Pull the parent /api/v2/files POST from web logs to confirm the path-traversal sequence. Step 2 — Contain: Stop the Langflow service (systemctl stop langflow), quarantine the host network connectivity, snapshot the disk for forensics. Remove the dropped file ONLY after capturing it. Step 3 — Hunt: List all files written by the Langflow process in the prior 30 days outside the data dir; review crontab and systemd unit listings; check authorized_keys across all users; review outbound network connections from python/uvicorn for C2; cross-check the source IP from the triggering POST against threat intel (especially MuddyWater infra per CVE-2025-3248 linkage). Patch to Langflow 1.10.0 before bringing the host back online.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "langflow_base", "langflow.main", "langflow.__main__")
| extend PathLower = tolower(FolderPath)
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/cron"
    or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron"
    or (FolderPath has ".ssh" and FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or FullPath =~ "/etc/ld.so.preload"
    or (FolderPath startswith "/etc/systemd/system" and FileName endswith ".service")
    or FolderPath startswith "/etc/profile.d"
    or (FolderPath startswith "/var/www" and FileName has_any (".php", ".jsp", ".aspx", ".sh"))
    or FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/bin"
    or FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/sbin"
    or FolderPath startswith "/root"
    or FullPath =~ "/etc/sudoers"
    or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d"
| where not(PathLower has "/.langflow/" or PathLower has "/langflow/data/" or PathLower has "/app/data/" or PathLower has "/tmp/langflow")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FullPath, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256, FileSize, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "langflow_base", "langflow.main")
| extend PathLower = tolower(TargetFilePath)
| where PathLower startswith "/etc/cron"
    or PathLower startswith "/var/spool/cron"
    or (PathLower has "/.ssh/" and TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or PathLower == "/etc/ld.so.preload"
    or (PathLower startswith "/etc/systemd/system" and TargetFileName endswith ".service")
    or PathLower startswith "/etc/profile.d"
    or (PathLower startswith "/var/www" and TargetFileExtension in~ ("php", "jsp", "aspx", "sh"))
    or PathLower startswith "/usr/local/bin"
    or PathLower startswith "/usr/local/sbin"
    or PathLower startswith "/root/"
| where not(PathLower has "/.langflow/" or PathLower has "/langflow/data/" or PathLower has "/app/data/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Langflow Python Process Writing to System-Critical Paths (CVE-2026-5027)
id: 7a3e1d02-2c8f-4a59-b1f7-langflow5027f
status: experimental
description: Detects the Langflow python/uvicorn/gunicorn process writing files into cron, SSH key, web-root, ld.so.preload, systemd unit, or /usr/local/bin paths — consistent with post-exploitation persistence via CVE-2026-5027 path traversal.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/path-traversal-flaw-in-ai-dev-platform-langflow-exploited-in-attacks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.t1053.003
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|contains:
      - 'python'
      - 'uvicorn'
      - 'gunicorn'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'langflow'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|startswith:
      - '/etc/cron'
      - '/var/spool/cron/'
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/etc/profile.d/'
      - '/usr/local/bin/'
      - '/usr/local/sbin/'
      - '/root/'
  selection_specific:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/etc/ld.so.preload'
      - '/etc/sudoers'
  selection_keyfile:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_langflow_data:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/.langflow/'
      - '/langflow/data/'
      - '/app/data/'
      - '/tmp/langflow'
  condition: selection_process and (selection_path or selection_specific or selection_keyfile) and not filter_langflow_data
falsepositives:
  - Langflow plugins legitimately writing to user-config paths during first-run setup
  - Operator running pip install / package upgrade inside the Langflow venv that writes to /usr/local/bin
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH (@process.name:(*python* OR *python3* OR *uvicorn* OR *gunicorn*)) @process.command_line:*langflow* (@file.path:(/etc/cron* OR /var/spool/cron/* OR /etc/ld.so.preload OR /etc/systemd/system/* OR /etc/profile.d/* OR /usr/local/bin/* OR /usr/local/sbin/* OR /root/* OR */.ssh/authorized_keys OR /var/www/*\.php OR /var/www/*\.jsp)) -@file.path:(*\/\.langflow\/* OR *\/langflow\/data\/* OR *\/tmp\/langflow*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)/i
| regex("langflow", field=ContextProcessCmdLine, strict=false) OR regex("langflow", field=CommandLine, strict=false)
| TargetFileName=/^(\/etc\/cron|\/var\/spool\/cron\/|\/etc\/ld\.so\.preload$|\/etc\/systemd\/system\/.*\.service$|\/etc\/profile\.d\/|\/usr\/local\/s?bin\/|\/root\/|.*\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$|\/var\/www\/.*\.(php|jsp|aspx|sh)$)/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/(\/\.langflow\/|\/langflow\/data\/|\/app\/data\/|\/tmp\/langflow)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[count(as=writes), min(@timestamp, as=first_seen), max(@timestamp, as=last_seen)])
| sort(writes, order=desc)

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma 72-hour monitor persistence via systemd user service or LaunchAgent · [LLM] Miasma AI coding tool config poisoning via non-IDE writer · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Miasma dead-man-switch destructive home directory wipe · [LLM] Miasma developer credential file harvest fan-out · [LLM] AWS SSM cross-host fan-out from a developer IAM principal
Miasma dead-man-switch destructive home directory wipe AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact destructive payload the Miasma monitor executes when the stolen GitHub token is revoked: a chained `rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`. This is the worm's burn-down trigger, fires on Linux and macOS developer hosts. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim destructive command in code block [1] of the article (`rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`). The two-tier rm chain on `~` plus `~/Documents` in a single command line is a fingerprint of the dead-man switch — legitimate cleanup never deletes the entire home and then re-deletes Documents. Corroborated with SafeDep and Cloudsmith write-ups of the same dead-man-switch logic in the dropped systemd/LaunchAgent monitor. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/ • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-worm-hits-73-microsoft-github.html
ATT&CKT1485 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer factory-resetting a personal VM with a bootstrap script that wipes home before re-cloning dotfiles
  • Test-harness teardown on a CI sandbox host that destroys the runner's home directory
  • An IR/forensics analyst executing a documented host-wipe runbook prior to re-imaging
  • A frustrated dev running the command interactively as a joke after a bad merge
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("image-builder","packer","cloud-init")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/var/lib/cloud"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "vm-rebuild"
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the originating process tree — the parent should be the Miasma monitor (`systemd --user` service or `launchd` LaunchAgent) launched within the last 72 hours; correlate the AccountName with recent api.github.com PAT activity. Contain: Immediately freeze the user's GitHub PAT (the revocation IS the trigger — but the destruction is already running, so isolate the host from network and snapshot disk before the worm finishes recursing). Hunt: across the fleet for sibling systemd user services or LaunchAgents created in the same window referencing api.github.com token-validity polling; pivot on the user's GitHub identity to find other developer hosts where the same PAT was used.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "rm -rf" and ProcessCommandLine has "Documents"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/?\s*(;|&&|\||\n)"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/Documents"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs in~ ("Linux","macOS","Darwin")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "rm -rf" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "Documents"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/?\s*(;|&&|\|)"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/Documents"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Worm Dead-Man-Switch Home Directory Wipe
id: 7b1e9f2a-3a8c-4d10-9c5d-3bd7d6c0f211
description: Detects the exact destructive chained rm -rf command Miasma executes when its stolen GitHub PAT is revoked (rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents). Triggered by the systemd user service or LaunchAgent monitor installed by the worm.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/
  - https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/
  - https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:

    CommandLine|re: '(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/?\s*(;|&&|\|).*rm\s+-rf\s+(~|\$HOME)/Documents'
  condition: selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Factory-reset scripts run on freshly-imaged developer VMs
  - Sandbox teardown automation
level: critical
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*"rm -rf ~/"* OR *"rm -rf $HOME/"*) AND @process.command_line:(*"rm -rf ~/Documents"* OR *"rm -rf $HOME/Documents"*)) -@process.executable.path:(/usr/lib/snapd/* OR /var/lib/cloud/instance/scripts/*)
#event_simpleName=/^(Synthetic)?ProcessRollup2$/
| regex("(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+(~|\\$HOME)/?\\s*(;|&&|\\|)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+(~|\\$HOME)/Documents", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
