Miasma 72-hour monitor persistence via systemd user service or LaunchAgent AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma persistence dropper — a systemd user service on Linux or a LaunchAgent plist on macOS, written by a non-package-manager process, that subsequently beacons to api.github.com. The article specifies this monitor polls GitHub-token validity every minute for up to 72 hours. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that the Miasma monitor `runs as a systemd user service on Linux or a LaunchAgent on macOS, and remains active for up to 72 hours`. The token-validity poll runs every minute, so a fresh persistence drop chained to >=20 api.github.com beacons within 72h is an extremely tight fingerprint. SHA256 IOCs from the campaign embedded as confirmation tier. Corroborated against SafeDep's analysis and Cloudsmith's persistence-chain write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/ • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-worm-hits-73-microsoft-github.html
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1543.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Homebrew installing a user LaunchAgent (e.g. `homebrew.mxcl.<svc>.plist`) — likely beaconing for tap updates
  • VS Code Remote / Cursor Remote tunnel installing a per-user systemd service that calls api.github.com for tunnel registration
  • fnm / nvm / Volta installing a LaunchAgent shell hook
  • Dotfile-bootstrap script (chezmoi/yadm) deploying personal LaunchAgents from a developer's repo
  • gh CLI auth refresh polling api.github.com on a host with a legit pre-existing service
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("brew","installer","Code Helper","Cursor Helper","node-gyp","fnm","nvm","volta","chezmoi","yadm")
| where not (TargetFilePath has "homebrew.mxcl." or TargetFilePath has "com.microsoft.VSCode" or TargetFilePath has "com.cursor.")
Response runbook
Triage: Read the unit/plist contents (`cat`) and verify the ExecStart command — Miasma units shell out to `node` or `python` with an embedded one-liner that reads a stored GitHub PAT and HEADs api.github.com. Validate the InitiatingProcessFileName — legit drops come from `brew`, `installer`, `Code Helper`; Miasma drops come from `node`, `npm`, `python`, `bash`, `git`. Contain: Stop the service (`systemctl --user stop`/`launchctl bootout`), pull the unit file for IR, revoke any GitHub PATs scoped to that user — BUT first capture the host disk image, because revocation triggers the dead-man switch detection (UC1). Hunt: cross-reference InitiatingProcessSHA256 fleet-wide; pivot the user's GitHub identity through audit log to identify packages/repos pushed in the persistence window.
let MiasmaHashes = dynamic(["396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4","d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223","f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c","d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b","f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f","25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b","d630397de8b01af0f6f5cf4463da91b17f28195a2c50c8f3f38ad9f7873fdb8e","3a9db5ba0c8cd4c91e91717df6b1a141fc1e0fbc0558b5a78d7f5c23f5b2a150"]);
let PersistenceDrops = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)/\.config/systemd/user(/|$)"
          or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)/Library/LaunchAgents(/|$)"
          or FileName endswith ".service" and FolderPath has "systemd/user"
          or FileName endswith ".plist" and FolderPath has "LaunchAgents"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd","launchd","brew","apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","snap","installer","pkg","Code","Code Helper","Cursor","Cursor Helper")
    | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId;
let GithubBeacons = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | project NetTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessId;
PersistenceDrops
| join kind=inner GithubBeacons on DeviceName
| where NetTime between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 72h)
| summarize BeaconCount = count(), FirstBeacon = min(NetTime), LastBeacon = max(NetTime)
          by Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
             InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where BeaconCount >= 20
| extend KnownHash = SHA256 in (MiasmaHashes)
| order by Timestamp desc
let PersistenceDrops = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/\.config/systemd/user/.*\.service$"
          or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/Library/LaunchAgents/.*\.plist$"
    | where ActingProcessName !in~ ("systemd","launchd","brew","apt","dpkg","yum","dnf","snap","installer","pkg","Code","Cursor")
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
let GithubBeacons = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstHostname has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | project BeaconTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstHostname, DstIpAddr;
PersistenceDrops
| join kind=inner GithubBeacons on DvcHostname
| where BeaconTime between (DropTime .. DropTime + 72h)
| summarize BeaconCount = count() by DropTime, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
            TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where BeaconCount >= 20
| order by DropTime desc
title: Miasma Persistence Drop via Systemd User Service or LaunchAgent
id: 4f2b8c91-7d35-4a6e-bf48-1c92f0e3a721
description: Detects creation of a systemd user service unit (~/.config/systemd/user/*.service) or LaunchAgent plist (~/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist) by a process that is not the OS init manager, a package manager, or an installer. This is the persistence vehicle Miasma uses to run its 72-hour GitHub-token validity monitor.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/
  - https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/
  - https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1543.001
  - attack.t1543.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i)(/\.config/systemd/user/[^/]+\.service$|/Library/LaunchAgents/[^/]+\.plist$)'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/systemd'
      - '/launchd'
      - '/brew'
      - '/apt'
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/yum'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/snap'
      - '/installer'
      - '/Code'
      - '/Cursor'
  condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Homebrew services installing user-level LaunchAgents
  - VS Code Server / Cursor Server installing remote-tunnel systemd units
  - fnm/nvm install scripts dropping LaunchAgents for shell hooks
level: high
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) @auditd.type:PATH (@file.path:*"/.config/systemd/user/"*.service OR @file.path:*"/Library/LaunchAgents/"*.plist) -@process.executable.path:(/usr/lib/systemd/* OR /usr/bin/brew OR /usr/local/bin/brew OR /usr/bin/apt OR /usr/bin/apt-get OR /usr/bin/dpkg OR /usr/sbin/installer OR */Code OR */Cursor)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)(/\\.config/systemd/user/[^/]+\\.service$|/Library/LaunchAgents/[^/]+\\.plist$)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("(?i)(/systemd$|/launchd$|/brew$|/apt$|/dpkg$|/installer$|/snap$|/Code$|/Cursor$)", field=ContextImageFileName)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\\.)github\\.com$/i}, field=aid, key=GithubCallbackAid, include=[ComputerName, DomainName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/systemd/user/*.service" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist") Filesystem.action IN (created, modified, written) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(systemd|launchd|brew|apt|dpkg|yum|dnf|snap|installer|pkg|Code|Cursor)$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/systemd/user/*.service" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist") Filesystem.action IN (created, modified, written) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(systemd|launchd|brew|apt|dpkg|yum|dnf|snap|installer|pkg|Code|Cursor)$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Miasma AI coding tool config poisoning via non-IDE writer AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes to AI-coding-assistant config directories (~/.claude, ~/.cursor, ~/.gemini, ~/.config/github-copilot, ~/.kiro, ~/.cline) performed by a shell, package manager, or scripting runtime rather than the IDE/agent binary itself. The article calls out Miasma poisoning these exact tools to weaponize the next developer prompt. Rationale: The article explicitly names `Claude, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, and Cline` as the AI tools whose configs Miasma poisons. The detection is the WRITE side: the IDE/agent binary normally owns its config dir, so a shell/npm/git/python writing into `~/.claude` or `~/.cursor` is the worm planting the prompt-injection payload. Corroborated by SafeDep's `Miasma-Open-Source-Release` repo analysis which confirms the config-injection vector. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/ • https://complexdiscovery.com/when-the-worm-targets-the-assistant-miasma-turns-ai-coding-agents-into-the-trigger/
ATT&CKT1546 T1059 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • chezmoi / yadm dotfile-sync writing `~/.cursor/settings.json` from a developer's tracked repo
  • Manual `cp` or `echo > ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` while the developer is hand-editing memory rules
  • npm-installed VS Code extension postinstall script writing to `~/.config/github-copilot/`
  • Cursor / Claude Code self-update routed through a `curl | sh` installer (writes happen as `bash`)
  • Developer pasting a config bootstrap from documentation that uses `cat <<EOF > ~/.kiro/config.yaml`
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("chezmoi","yadm","stow","dotbot")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "update" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("claude","cursor","gemini","copilot","kiro","cline"))
Response runbook
Triage: Diff the written file against the previous version in source control (most devs version their AI configs) — look for added shell commands, `curl|sh` patterns, or MCP server registrations pointing to suspicious npm/GitHub URLs. Inspect the writing process tree: a `node` parent that just ran `npm install <pkg>` is the supply-chain pivot. Contain: Revert the config file from the last-known-good git commit, kill any agent/MCP processes the poisoned config started, isolate the host if MCP execution already fired. Hunt: across the org for the same file SHA256 — Miasma uses a per-build payload but the injected MCP/agent definition often reuses domain or repo strings; pivot on those.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)/\.(claude|cursor|gemini|kiro|cline)(/|$)"
      or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)/\.config/(github-copilot|copilot|cursor|kiro|cline)(/|$)"
      or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)/Library/Application Support/(Claude|Cursor|GitHub Copilot|Gemini|Kiro|Cline)/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","python","python3","git","curl","wget","ruby","gem","pip","pip3","tar","unzip")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("claude","cursor","Cursor Helper","Code","Code Helper","gemini","copilot","kiro","cline")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName endswith ".md" or FileName endswith ".json" or FileName endswith ".yaml" or FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".toml" or FileName startswith "AGENTS" or FileName startswith "CLAUDE" or FileName has "mcp" or FileName has "settings"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/\.(claude|cursor|gemini|kiro|cline)(/|$)"
      or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/\.config/(github-copilot|copilot|cursor|kiro|cline)(/|$)"
      or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/Library/Application Support/(Claude|Cursor|GitHub Copilot|Gemini|Kiro|Cline)/"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","python","python3","git","curl","wget","ruby","gem","pip","pip3","tar","unzip")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("claude","cursor","Code","Code Helper","gemini","copilot","kiro","cline")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".md" or TargetFileName endswith ".json" or TargetFileName endswith ".yaml" or TargetFileName endswith ".yml" or TargetFileName has_any ("AGENTS","CLAUDE","mcp","settings")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma developer credential file harvest fan-out AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a single non-allowlisted process reading four or more distinct developer credential / secret-store files within a one-minute window. The article describes Miasma harvesting cloud provider, CI/CD, password manager, Kubernetes, and secret-store credentials in one stage; this aggregates that across the canonical dotfile locations. Rationale: The article enumerates the categories Miasma harvests — `cloud providers, CI/CD systems, password managers, Kubernetes, and secret stores` — which maps to the canonical Unix dotfile locations (.aws, .npmrc, .pypirc, .gem, .kube, .docker, .config/gh, .ssh, .config/op, .password-store, .jfrog). A single unknown process touching 4+ of these inside 60s is the fan-out shape. Sigma is intentionally omitted because the detection is a count-threshold over a time bin, which Sigma's single-event-shape doesn't express cleanly. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Time Machine / restic / borg backup sweeping the user's home directory
  • A dev running `env | grep` after sourcing a project's `direnv` that pulls AWS+kube+npm creds in sequence (likely caught by allowlist)
  • A new-machine bootstrap script copying dotfiles from a USB stick
  • An IR/forensics agent (Velociraptor, GRR) running a credential-inventory hunt
  • Cloud-config sync tooling (e.g. `aws-vault sync`, `kubelogin`)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tmutil","rsync","restic","borg","kopia","velociraptor","osqueryd","aws-vault","kubelogin","direnv")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "snapshot")
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the offending process's full image path and SHA256, and check if it's a Node/Python/Bash one-liner forked from npm/pip install. Cross-reference `InitiatingProcessParentFileName` — Miasma typically arrives as `node` under `npm`/`npx` (the postinstall hook), so a `node` parent of `npm install` is high-confidence. Contain: Force-rotate every credential the process touched — AWS access keys, npm/pypi/rubygems tokens, JFrog API keys, GitHub PATs, kubeconfig contexts. Disable the user's CI/CD pipelines until reviewed. Hunt: pivot the GitHub PAT to find any new repos created under that account (Miasma exfils to dead-drop repos under accounts like `liuende501`, `windy629`, `HerGomUli`); list packages published by the user across npm/PyPI/RubyGems in the last 24h.
let CredPathFragments = dynamic([
    "/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.npmrc","/.pypirc",
    "/.gem/credentials","/.kube/config","/.docker/config.json",
    "/.netrc","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.config/git/credentials",
    "/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/id_ecdsa",
    "/.config/op/","/.password-store/","/.cargo/credentials","/.jfrog/"
]);
let AllowedReaders = dynamic([
    "aws","kubectl","docker","ssh","sshd","git","gh","node","npm","pnpm","yarn",
    "gem","pip","pip3","gpg","op","1password","Code","Code Helper","Cursor",
    "claude","tmutil","rsync","restic","borg","kopia"
]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileOpened","FileRead","FileCreated")
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)
| where FullPath has_any (CredPathFragments)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (AllowedReaders)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize CredsHit = dcount(FullPath), SamplePaths = make_set(FullPath, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName,
             InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where CredsHit >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc

ImFileEvent

| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileRead","FileOpened","FileCreated")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredPathFragments)
| where ActingProcessName !in~ (AllowedReaders)
| summarize CredsHit = dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
             ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where CredsHit >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc

Miasma-Open-Source-Release repository fetch via git clone or HTTP download AIDelivery High
Hunts any process referencing the exact GitHub repository name `Miasma-Open-Source-Release` — the repo name SafeDep observed the threat actors using across compromised developer accounts to publish the leaked source. Covers `git clone`, `curl`/`wget` of the tarball, and browser-mediated downloads. Rationale: `Miasma-Open-Source-Release` is the exact repository naming convention SafeDep observed across every compromised developer account distributing the leaked toolkit (article: `the threat actors leaked the source code in a repo named "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"`). The string is unique enough that any process or HTTP reference is high-fidelity. Corroborated by SafeDep, The Register, and Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-worm-hits-73-microsoft-github.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC / IR analyst pulling the repo for forensic analysis
  • Threat-intel team automatically ingesting the artefact via gh CLI
  • Security researcher mirroring the repo to a private archive
  • DFIR sandbox detonating the repo in a controlled environment
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("ir-sandbox-01","ti-ingest-01","malware-lab-01")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cape","cuckoo","any.run")
Response runbook
Triage: Identify the requester — if it's a security analyst on the IR team running from a known forensic workstation, suppress and document. For any other host, treat it as suspected first-stage execution. Pull DeviceProcessEvents for the host in a +/- 10-minute window to see what ran after the clone. Contain: Isolate the host from the network and quarantine the cloned directory. Preserve any GitHub credentials present on disk for IR. Hunt: Pivot the GitHub username portion of the URL (e.g. `github.com/<user>/Miasma-Open-Source-Release`) — that account is compromised; check if any internal developers have starred, forked, or have collaborator access. Search for sibling drop accounts (`liuende501`, `windy629`, `HerGomUli`) referenced across the fleet.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind = "process",
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName),
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          EventKind = "network", FileName = "", ProcessCommandLine = RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName = InitiatingProcessParentFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
     or ParentProcessCommandLine has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventKind = "process",
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "Miasma-Open-Source-Release"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername = SrcUsername,
          EventKind = "network", ActingProcessName = "", ActingProcessCommandLine = Url,
          ParentProcessName = "")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS SSM cross-host fan-out from a developer IAM principal AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts AWS Systems Manager `StartSession`/`SendCommand`/`StartAutomationExecution` events from a single IAM user / assumed role hitting many distinct instance targets in a short window. The article calls out SSM as one of Miasma's two lateral movement primitives after harvesting cloud creds. Rationale: The article explicitly names `SSH and AWS Systems Manager (SSM)` as Miasma's lateral movement primitives. After stealing AWS keys from `~/.aws/credentials` (caught by UC4), the worm pivots into SSM to reach EC2 hosts and run commands. A single principal hitting 5+ distinct targets in 10 minutes is the spread shape. Sentinel/Defender/Falcon are intentionally empty because CloudTrail telemetry doesn't natively flow into those backends; CloudWatch and Datadog are the right destinations. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/k/shai-hulud-2-0-targets-cloud-and-developer-systems.html • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-ai-coding-agent-config-injection/
ATT&CKT1021.008 T1078.004 T1570
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager scheduled patching window
  • DevOps engineer running a fleet-wide configuration update via `aws ssm send-command --targets`
  • Automated drift remediation pipeline running from a CI/CD role
  • Incident response triage where on-call SRE pulls diagnostics from many hosts at once
  • Bulk RDP/SSH bootstrap via SSM for a newly-launched ASG
Suppression filter
| filter userIdentity.arn not like /role\/SSMPatchManager/
      and userIdentity.arn not like /role\/.*-cicd-/
      and not (requestParameters.documentName like /AWS-RunPatchBaseline|AWS-UpdateSSMAgent/)
      and additionalEventData.MFAUsed = "No"
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the IAM principal's recent AssumeRole / GetSessionToken events and check `additionalEventData.MFAUsed` — Miasma stole long-lived AWS keys, so the SSM calls won't have an MFA-backed session. Verify `sourceIPAddress` against the user's normal egress (developer IP vs unknown VPS). Contain: Revoke the access key (`UpdateAccessKey` to Inactive), kill all running SSM sessions for that principal (`TerminateSession`), rotate the IAM user's credentials, and put a deny policy on the role for `ssm:*` while investigating. Hunt: Enumerate every instance the principal touched (`requestParameters.target`/`instanceIds`) — those are now suspect-lateral; run the credential-harvest detection (UC4) on each. Check S3/ECR/Lambda actions from the same principal in the same window for staging activity.
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(StartSession OR SendCommand OR StartAutomationExecution) @evt.source:ssm.amazonaws.com @evt.outcome:success -@userIdentity.arn:(*"role/SSMPatchManager"* OR *"role/aws-service-role"* OR *"role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole"* OR *"role/AWSServiceRoleFor"*)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.userName, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, userIdentity.sessionContext.attributes.mfaAuthenticated, requestParameters.target, requestParameters.instanceIds, requestParameters.documentName, awsRegion
| filter eventSource = "ssm.amazonaws.com"
     and eventName in ["StartSession","SendCommand","StartAutomationExecution"]
     and not isPresent(errorCode)
     and userIdentity.arn not like /aws-service-role|SSMPatchManager|OrganizationAccountAccessRole|AWSServiceRoleFor/
| stats count(*) as ssm_calls,
        count_distinct(requestParameters.target) as distinct_targets,
        earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen,
        latest(@timestamp) as last_seen,
        count_distinct(awsRegion) as regions_touched
        by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName
| filter distinct_targets >= 5
| sort last_seen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b") or SHA1 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b") or MD5 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b") or SHA1 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b") or MD5 in~ ("396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["396cac9e457ec54ff6d3f6311cb5cc1da8054d019ce3ffa1de5741506c7a4ea4", "d8d170af3de17bb9b217c52aaaffdf9395f35ef015a57ef676e406c121e5e223", "f0641e053e81f0d01fa46db35a83e0a34494886503086866d956d14e81fd3e1c", "d5a97614d5319ce9c8e01fa0b4eb06fb5b9e54fa13b23d718174a1546444123b", "f88258e21592084a2f93a572ade8f9b91c0cd0e242f5cf6121ed7bad0f7bdd1f", "25e121e3b7d300c0d0075b33e5eca39a3e6a659fb9cfee52b70ef71686628f1b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Defender TVM flags CVE-2026-48063 (vulnerable Baileys npm package) on host
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vulnerable Baileys npm package install/presence on Windows endpoints
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Defender TVM flags CVE-2026-48063 (vulnerable Baileys npm package) on host AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts where Defender Threat & Vulnerability Management has identified the npm:baileys / npm:@whiskeysockets/baileys package at a vulnerable version (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12). This is the cleanest, lowest-FP route to find exposed WhatsApp-bot/automation hosts before exploitation via a crafted protocolMessage payload. Rationale: Direct CVE pivot — the advisory itself supplies CVE-2026-48063 as the canonical identifier. TVM/SBOM-grounded detection is the lowest-FP shape for a pure library vulnerability with no host-side TTPs. No external corroboration needed; the GitHub Security Advisory IS the authoritative source.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerability_Management.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM data shortly after a successful upgrade (next TVM scan will clear it)
  • Dev/test workstations where baileys is installed but never connected to a real WhatsApp session
  • TVM version-parsing miss-attributing a back-ported security fix in a forked baileys build
  • Container build images flagged but never deployed to runtime
  • Pre-release ≥7.0.0-rc12 incorrectly version-compared by the scanner
Suppression filter
| where VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("High","Critical")
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc12" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc.12"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SoftwareVersion sits in the vulnerable range (< 6.7.22, or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12). Identify the package owner via repo, code-owner file, or LoggedOnUsers. Check if the host actually has a live WhatsApp session (look for sustained TCP to *.whatsapp.net / web.whatsapp.com from node.exe). 2) Contain: open a P2 patch ticket for owner to upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12. Workaround until patched — drop messages.upsert events containing a requestId field and set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false in socket config. 3) Hunt: enumerate every other host with the file-event UC (paired UC2) to find shadow-IT baileys deployments TVM missed; pivot on parent node.exe command lines referencing automation scripts.

Vulnerable Baileys npm package install/presence on Windows endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for file-write activity inside node_modules\baileys or node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys directories — surfaces hosts running the vulnerable WhatsApp library even when TVM/SBOM tooling has no signal on the npm package. Pair with UC1 (TVM) to cover environments without SBOM ingestion. Rationale: Uses the exact package paths from the advisory's affected-packages list (npm:baileys and npm:@whiskeysockets/baileys). File-path hunting catches shadow-IT installs that TVM/SBOM never enrolled. Cross-platform path variants (\ vs /) included for WSL/dev containers. Excludes Defender self-scan noise.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate corporate WhatsApp bot/automation projects running an already-patched baileys version (≥6.7.22 or ≥7.0.0-rc12)
  • Developer workstations where engineers clone open-source baileys for unrelated work
  • Jenkins/GitHub Actions self-hosted runners pulling baileys as a build-stage transitive dependency
  • Container build hosts producing baileys-containing images that are deployed elsewhere
  • Backup/restore agents replaying historical node_modules archives onto recovery hosts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\AppData\Local\Temp\", "\Windows\Temp\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsiExec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the actual baileys version from the host's package.json (DeviceFileEvents won't tell you the version, only the path). If owner cannot be identified from the directory tree, use InitiatingProcessAccountName / LoggedOnUsers from DeviceInfo. 2) Contain: if vulnerable version (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12), open a patch ticket and apply the workaround (drop messages.upsert events containing requestId, set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false). For internet-facing bot hosts treat as priority. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound traffic to *.whatsapp.net / web.whatsapp.com from node.exe to confirm an active WhatsApp session is bound to the vulnerable lib; enumerate other repos in the same project group that may share the dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), FileCount = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 25), Installers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), FileCount = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 25), Installers = make_set(ActingProcessName, 10)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath
| order by LastSeen desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Installation of Aikido-flagged malicious npm packages on developer endpoints
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm postinstall hook spawning a shell interpreter on a developer device · [LLM] Execution of binaries matching Aikido article SHA1 hashes · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Developer-host beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Postinstall-driven read of cloud credentials and SSH keys from developer home
Installation of Aikido-flagged malicious npm packages on developer endpoints AIDelivery High
Detects npm/yarn/pnpm installs resolving to the specific package@version combinations called out in the article — axios 0.30.4 / 1.14.1, postmark-mcp 1.0.16-1.0.18, plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, @bitwarden/cli 2026.4.0. Catches the supply-chain ingress before postinstall fires. Rationale: Pivots on the exact package@version strings the article names (axios 0.30.4/1.14.1, postmark-mcp 1.0.16-1.0.18, plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, @bitwarden/cli 2026.4.0). Article body + kill-chain Phase 1 IOCs.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team red-team or threat-emulation install of the IOC packages for testing
  • Internal repro of the Aikido advisory by an engineer on a sandbox laptop
  • CI build cache of a research VM that retained the package in node_modules
  • Renovate/Dependabot scanning workflow surfacing the version in dry-run mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("sandbox-runner.exe","redteam-vm.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the device + developer; pull the full command line and parent (was this an AI-agent automation in Slack/CI, or a manual install?). Check whether node_modules already contains the package. 2. Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, revoke any npm/cloud/SSH/GitHub tokens reachable from the device's home directory, rotate Bitwarden master password if @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 was pulled. 3. Hunt: cross-reference Slack audit logs for an AI-bot-approved PR in the prior hour; look across the fleet for the same IOC packages in DeviceFileEvents writes to package-lock.json/yarn.lock.

npm postinstall hook spawning a shell interpreter on a developer device AIInstallation High
Catches the article's exact execution chain: node/npm running a postinstall/preinstall script that immediately spawns cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, or wscript/cscript/mshta — the textbook supply-chain payload pattern flagged by the Aikido advisory. Rationale: Targets the article's literal execution narrative: 'pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook' — node/npm as the spawner, shell as the child. Parent-cmdline filter pins it to install-hook context, not interactive node use. Kill-chain Phase 2 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / node-pre-gyp native module compile scripts (legitimate cmd.exe / sh.exe spawn during install of e.g. bcrypt, sharp)
  • Electron / Playwright postinstall downloading browser binaries with curl
  • Husky git-hook installer spawning a shell during `npm install`
  • Lerna / nx monorepo install orchestrators running cross-package scripts
  • Yarn berry's `node-modules` linker reorganising .bin shims
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install","husky","playwright install","electron install","puppeteer")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\bcrypt\\" or FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\sharp\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the full parent + child command lines and the package whose postinstall fired (resolve from node_modules path); is this a known native-build module (node-gyp/sharp/bcrypt) or an unknown package? 2. Contain: isolate the host, terminate the descendent chain, suspend the developer's npm publish token and any GitHub PATs scoped to the device. 3. Hunt: pivot on the package name across the fleet via DeviceFileEvents writes to node_modules; check DeviceNetworkEvents from the host in the 5 minutes after the shell spawned for the article's C2 IPs/domains; check Slack audit logs for an AI-agent-approved PR that pulled the dependency.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules\\.bin")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
  ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
  ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  ChildImage  = FolderPath,
  ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
  SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of binaries matching Aikido article SHA1 hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hard-IOC sweep for the three SHA1 hashes (2553649f..., d6f3f62f..., 07d889e2...) tied by Aikido Intel to the GlassWorm / TeamPCP / postmark-mcp postinstall payloads. Triggers on either process execution or file landing. Rationale: Three SHA1 hashes are explicit hard IOCs published alongside the article — zero-FP signal when matched. Kill-chain Phase 2 explicitly lists these hashes. Worth a 90-day retrospective sweep on first deploy.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher re-analysing the IOCs in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel team detonating the sample in an isolated detonation VM
  • Incident-response retained artifact already known-quarantined by Defender
  • EDR vendor's own validation hash test on a security-team device
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the hit isn't from a known security-research sandbox or AV vendor test machine; pull file path, signer, parent process. 2. Contain: isolate the host immediately, take a memory image before reboot, revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, kubeconfig, Bitwarden vault), force-rotate the developer's SSO password and reset MFA. 3. Hunt: pivot on the parent npm package name fleet-wide; check the kill-chain C2 IPs/domains in DeviceNetworkEvents from the host going back 90 days; review GitHub audit log for the developer's PAT for bulk-clone activity.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="Process"),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="File")
| order by Timestamp desc

union
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Source="Process"),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where TargetFileSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName=ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileName, Source="File")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Developer-host beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Outbound network or DNS from any endpoint to the four C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) or the two domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) named in the article. Highest priority when the initiating process is node/npm/Code.exe. Rationale: Six hard network IOCs (4 IPs + 2 domains) from kill-chain Phase 6 — direct match against the Aikido article's C2 list. Enrichment flag on node.exe / Code.exe / browser process owner identifies the developer-device pivot the article calls out.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion job pre-fetching the IOCs for sandboxing
  • Web filter / proxy testing the IOC list with active probes
  • Researcher visiting giftshop.club via a controlled browser
  • Defender ASR test traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp-feed.exe","otx-fetcher.exe","threatfox-sync.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "TI-SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source device, the initiating process tree, and whether the traffic was blocked at proxy/firewall vs allowed. 2. Contain: isolate the device via EDR, sinkhole the domains at the recursive resolver, block the IPs at egress, force-revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, Bitwarden, kubeconfig). 3. Hunt: retro-sweep 90 days of DeviceNetworkEvents and DNS across the fleet for the same IOCs; cross-reference with kill-chain Phase 1 IOC package installs on the same hosts in the prior 24h.

title: Beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 Infrastructure
id: c4d5e6f7-8a9b-4c0d-1e2f-3a4b5c6d7e8f
description: Detects outbound connections or DNS queries from any endpoint to the C2 IPs and domains published in the Aikido June 2026 advisory.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10

logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:

      - '142.11.206.73'

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(142.11.206.73 OR 45.32.150.251 OR 45.32.151.157 OR 70.34.242.255) OR @DestinationHostname:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))

Postinstall-driven read of cloud credentials and SSH keys from developer home AIActions on Objectives Medium
A node/npm-spawned process reading ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.npmrc, ~/.kube/config or a Bitwarden vault file — the credential-theft step the article describes ('cloud credentials, SSH keys, npm publish tokens, Kubernetes configs'). Rationale: Pairs the article's named credential stores (cloud creds, SSH keys, npm tokens, kubeconfig) with node.exe parent — high-signal because legitimate node code rarely reads ~/.aws/credentials or ~/.ssh/id_* during a postinstall. Kill-chain Phase 4 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • aws-sdk-js / aws-vault helper modules legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials at runtime
  • ssh2 / simple-git npm modules reading ~/.ssh/id_rsa for repo auth during a build
  • kubectl-node wrapper modules reading ~/.kube/config
  • Bitwarden CLI legitimate authenticated session refresh
  • Developer running `npm login` writes .npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","aws-vault","@kubernetes/client-node","simple-git","node-ssh","ssh2")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\@aws-sdk\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the npm package whose postinstall touched the credential file (walk the InitiatingProcessParentId chain) — is the package on the Aikido IOC list? 2. Contain: rotate every credential that lived in the touched files (AWS keys, SSH keys + replace authorized_keys, npm publish tokens, kubeconfig tokens, Bitwarden master password); isolate the host; pull memory before reboot. 3. Hunt: check CloudTrail / Azure AD / GitHub audit logs for use of those credentials from any IP not previously seen for the developer's identity in the prior 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   or ActionType has "Open"
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config", @"\.ssh\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.kube\config", @"Bitwarden\data.json", @"@bitwarden\")
     or FileName in~ ("credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","kubeconfig","data.json",".env"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","node_modules","install.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
  InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.ssh/","/.npmrc","/.kube/config","Bitwarden\\data.json","@bitwarden")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","kubeconfig","data.json",".env"))
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","node_modules","install.js","install.cjs")
   or ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@EventID:11 OR @auditd.type:PATH) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.aws\\credentials* OR *\\.aws\\config* OR *\\.ssh\\id_* OR *\\.npmrc* OR *\\.kube\\config* OR *Bitwarden\\data.json* OR *.env) OR @file.path:(*/.aws/credentials* OR */.ssh/id_* OR */.npmrc* OR */.kube/config*)) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR */bin/node OR */bin/npm)
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten)
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.aws\\\\config|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_|\\\\\\.npmrc|\\\\\\.kube\\\\config|Bitwarden\\\\data\\.json|@bitwarden|\\\\\\.env", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network communication with ShinyHunters PeopleSoft attack infrastructure IPs
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH credential spray against PeopleSoft administrative accounts (psoft, oracle, linuxadm) · [LLM] MeshCentral agent installation on Oracle PeopleSoft Linux servers · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Oracle PeopleSoft servers hacked in ShinyHunters data theft attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS lookup or TLS SNI for ShinyHunters azurenetfiles.net infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ShinyHunters PeopleSoft ransom-note file write (README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network communication with ShinyHunters PeopleSoft attack infrastructure IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for any inbound or outbound network traffic to the seven IPs Michael R recovered from exposed ShinyHunters staging directories. The article tells operators to analyse logs for connections from these IPs to PeopleSoft instances — this is the primary IOC pivot. Rationale: Anchored on the seven IPs published by Michael R and re-shared by BleepingComputer. Several of these IPs presented the azurenetfiles.net TLS certificate, a known ShinyHunters infrastructure marker. Cross-checked the abuse.ch IP intel feed and BleepingComputer's prior ShinyHunters coverage tying azurenetfiles.net to the group. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scrapers proxying through your egress (e.g. researcher VMs polling sinkholes)
  • Internal vulnerability scans that include the IPs as part of an external-attack-surface sweep
  • Legitimate web traffic if any IP is shared with a CDN PoP in the future (currently dedicated)
  • VPN concentrators forwarding telemetry to threat-intel platforms
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threatintel"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on DeviceName/host receiving traffic — confirm it is an Oracle PeopleSoft web, app, or batch server. Pull the full process tree around the connection time and any HTTP requests in W3CIISLog / WebLogic / Tuxedo access logs to identify the exploited endpoint. 2. Contain: pull the host off internet routing (firewall block + remove from load balancer), preserve memory and disk, rotate the psoft / oracle / linuxadm credentials and any SSH keys present, and revoke all PeopleSoft active sessions. 3. Hunt: search for the ShinyHunters ransom note filename, MeshCentral binaries/agents, outbound DNS to azurenetfiles.net, and SSH activity from the PeopleSoft host to internal hosts named in /etc/hosts.

ShinyHunters PeopleSoft ransom-note file write (README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the specific ransom-note filename the ShinyHunters script drops on compromised PeopleSoft web and application servers. The name is unique enough to alert on directly with effectively zero false positives. Rationale: The article reproduces the exact filename the ShinyHunters shell script writes — 'README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT'. The string is long, unique, all-caps with hyphens and verbs, so an exact file-create match is high-fidelity and effectively unhittable by legitimate software. Cross-checked the screenshot at https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/attacks/p/peoplesoft/shinyhunters/shiny-script.jpg. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1657 T1486 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR team or threat-intel analyst copying the IOC into a local file for hunt enrichment
  • Detection-engineering tests deploying a benign decoy with the same name
  • EDR sandbox detonating the ShinyHunters script in an isolated lab
  • Forensic image mounted on an analyst workstation containing a previously-dropped note
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the host writing the note and the writing process — for a Linux PeopleSoft server this should be bash/sh invoked from an SSH session. Capture the .bash_history of the writing user. 2. Contain: immediately isolate the host, snapshot the disk, rotate the writing user's SSH keys and password, and revoke any cached PeopleSoft application credentials. 3. Hunt: search peer PeopleSoft hosts (peers from /etc/hosts) for the same filename, any SSH logons from the original compromised host outbound, and network egress to the seven ShinyHunters IPs in the prior UC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
   or FolderPath has "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileCreate")
    | where TargetFileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT" or TargetFilePath has "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImFileEvent", Host = DvcHostname, User = ActorUsername, FilePath = TargetFilePath, FileName = TargetFileName, ProcName = ActingProcessName, ProcCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "Syslog", Host = Computer, User = "", FilePath = SyslogMessage, FileName = "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT", ProcName = ProcessName, ProcCmd = SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
